stimuli.title: Surviving in the Desert
stimuli.text:
Desert plants face a simple problem: rain is rare, but the sun is strong almost every day. Many of them solve it by storing water. A cactus, for example, has a thick stem that swells after a storm and slowly shrinks during the long dry months that follow. Its leaves have been reduced to spines, which lose far less water than broad leaves and also discourage thirsty animals from taking a bite.

Timing matters as well. Most plants open the tiny pores on their surface during the day to take in carbon dioxide, but every open pore also lets water escape. Many cacti reverse this pattern. They open their pores at night, when the air is cooler and more humid, store the carbon dioxide in a chemical form, and use it for photosynthesis the next day with their pores tightly closed.

Other desert plants avoid the dry season altogether. Their seeds can lie in the soil for years. When a heavy rain finally arrives, they sprout, flower and produce new seeds within a few weeks, long before the ground dries out again.

stimuli.title: Why Leaves Change Color
stimuli.text:
In many parts of the world, the leaves of trees turn yellow, orange or red in autumn. The colors do not appear suddenly. Most of them are in the leaf all summer, but they are hidden.

During the growing season, leaves are full of chlorophyll, the green substance that plants use to turn sunlight into food. There is so much chlorophyll that its green covers the other colors. As the days grow shorter and cooler in autumn, the tree stops making new chlorophyll. The green slowly breaks down, and the yellow and orange colors that were there all along begin to show.

Red is different. Some trees, such as certain maples, make new red substances in their leaves in autumn. Bright, sunny days and cool nights help them make more, so the reds are usually strongest in autumns with that kind of weather.

After the colors appear, the tree forms a thin layer of cells where each leaf joins its branch. This layer cuts the leaf off from the tree, and the leaf falls. The tree can then rest through the winter without losing water through its leaves.

stimuli.title: Paint in a Tube
stimuli.text:
For centuries, European painters prepared their own colors in the studio. They ground pigments into powder and mixed them with oil shortly before use, because the paint dried quickly once exposed to air. Prepared paint could be stored for a short time in pieces of animal bladder tied with string, but these leaked, burst and were awkward to carry. Painting a landscape therefore usually meant sketching outdoors and finishing the picture indoors.

In 1841 the American portrait painter John Goffe Rand patented a small, squeezable metal tube with a screw cap. The tube kept paint fresh for long periods and could be closed after each use. Color manufacturers soon adopted it, and by the middle of the century a painter could buy a full range of ready-made colors and pack them in a box.

The tube did not create a new style by itself, but it removed a practical obstacle. The French Impressionists of the 1870s, who wanted to record how light and weather changed from hour to hour, could now complete entire canvases in the open air. Some of them later acknowledged that their way of working would have been difficult, if not impossible, without paint that traveled well.

stimuli.title: Hunting by Sound
stimuli.text:
Most bats hunt at night, when insects are plentiful and few birds compete for them. To find prey in the dark, many species rely on echolocation. A bat produces a series of short, high-pitched calls, most of them far above the range of human hearing, and listens for the echoes that bounce back from objects around it. The time an echo takes to return tells the bat how far away an object is, and small differences between the sound reaching its left and right ears reveal the object's direction.

The calls change as a hunt progresses. While searching, a bat calls only a few times per second, which lets it scan a wide area. Once it detects an insect, it calls faster and faster, and just before the catch the calls may come close to two hundred times per second. This final burst gives the bat rapid updates on the exact position of a moving target.

Insects are not defenseless. Some moths can hear bat calls and dive toward the ground when a bat approaches, and a few species even produce clicking sounds of their own that seem to interfere with the bat's ability to judge distance.

stimuli.title: Supply and Demand
stimuli.text:
Why does the price of strawberries change during the year? Economists answer this kind of question with two ideas: supply and demand.

Supply is the amount of a product that sellers are ready to sell. Demand is the amount that buyers want to buy. When a product is scarce but many people want it, buyers compete with one another, and the price goes up. When there is more of a product than people want, sellers lower the price to attract buyers.

Strawberries are a good example. In early summer, farms near a city harvest large amounts of fruit at the same time. The supply is high, so shops lower their prices to sell the berries before they spoil. In winter, the fruit must come from far away, which costs more, and there is less of it in the shops. Even if people want strawberries just as much as in summer, the lower supply pushes the price up.

Prices also send signals. A high price tells farmers that buyers will pay well for a product, so some farmers decide to grow more of it the next year.

stimuli.title: The Dust Bowl
stimuli.text:
During the 1930s, the southern Great Plains of the United States suffered a disaster that came to be known as the Dust Bowl. Its causes were partly natural and partly human. In the preceding decades, rising wheat prices and new tractors had encouraged farmers to plow millions of acres of native grassland. The deep roots of those grasses had anchored the light soil through earlier dry periods; plowed fields, by contrast, were often left bare between harvests.

When a severe drought began in the early 1930s, crops failed and the exposed soil dried to powder. Strong winds then lifted it into enormous clouds, some of which carried dust as far as the Atlantic coast. Many families, unable to farm or repay their debts, abandoned their land and moved west in search of work.

The crisis also changed how the federal government approached farming. In 1935 Congress created the Soil Conservation Service, which promoted methods such as planting rows of trees to break the wind, plowing along the natural curves of the land, and returning damaged fields to grass. These practices were intended not merely to repair the damage but to prevent a repetition.

stimuli.title: Tides
stimuli.text:
Along most coastlines, the level of the sea rises and falls about twice a day. These changes, called tides, are caused mainly by the gravity of the Moon. The Moon pulls most strongly on the side of the Earth that faces it, so the ocean there bulges slightly toward the Moon. A second bulge forms on the opposite side of the planet, where the Moon's pull is weakest. As the Earth turns, a given coast passes through both bulges, which is why it usually has two high tides and two low tides each day.

The Sun affects tides too, though its effect is less than half as strong because it is so much farther away. When the Sun and the Moon line up, at new moon and full moon, their pulls combine, and the difference between high and low water is largest. These are called spring tides, although they have nothing to do with the season. When the Sun and Moon pull at right angles, the tidal range is smallest; these are neap tides.

The shape of a coast can greatly increase the range. In some narrow bays, the water rises many meters between low and high tide.

stimuli.title: The Power of Defaults
stimuli.text:
When people face a choice, they often stick with whatever option is already selected for them. Economists and psychologists call this preselected option the default, and research suggests that defaults can strongly shape behavior even when changing them takes only a moment.

Retirement savings offer a well-known example. At some companies, new employees must actively sign up to join the savings plan; at others, they are enrolled automatically and must fill out a form if they wish to leave. Studies of such companies have found that participation is far higher when joining is the default, although the plan, the benefits and the effort needed to switch are almost identical.

Researchers suggest several reasons. Making a decision requires attention, and people may postpone a choice that seems complicated. Some people also interpret the default as a recommendation, assuming that whoever set it had good reasons. Finally, people tend to feel a loss more sharply than an equal gain, so giving up the current option can feel like a loss.

Because defaults are so influential, those who design forms and programs carry a responsibility to choose them with care.

stimuli.title: The Beginnings of Jazz
stimuli.text:
Jazz developed in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and the city of New Orleans played a central part in its birth. As a busy port, the city brought together people of African, European and Caribbean backgrounds, along with their musical traditions. Brass bands marched in parades and at funerals, dance halls hired small groups to play late into the night, and church choirs, work songs and the blues all contributed sounds and rhythms.

Early jazz musicians borrowed from all of these sources, but they also changed how the music was played. Instead of following a written score note for note, players often improvised, creating new melodies on the spot. In a typical early jazz band, the cornet or trumpet carried the main tune while the clarinet and trombone wove lines around it, so that several melodies sounded at once.

The new music did not stay in one city. Beginning around the time of the First World War, many musicians moved north to cities such as Chicago and New York, and records and radio carried their playing to listeners who had never heard a live jazz band.

stimuli.title: How Vaccines Work
stimuli.text:
The human immune system learns from experience. When a germ enters the body for the first time, the immune system needs several days to recognize it and produce antibodies, proteins that attach to the germ and help destroy it. During that time the person may become seriously ill. Afterward, however, some immune cells remain in the body as memory cells. If the same germ returns, these cells respond much faster, often before any symptoms appear.

Vaccines take advantage of this memory. A vaccine exposes the immune system to a harmless version or a single part of a germ, such as a surface protein. Because this material cannot cause the disease, the person does not become sick, yet the immune system still learns to recognize the germ and forms memory cells.

Some vaccines provide protection for life, while others need booster doses because memory fades or because the germ changes over time. When enough people in a community are immune, a germ has trouble spreading from person to person. This also protects people who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborn babies.

options: They fall before the other leaves
Their color is made new in autumn
They appear only in warm autumns
Their color is in the leaf all summer
questions.explanation: Some trees "make new red substances in their leaves in autumn", while yellow and orange are present all summer.

questions.stem: Which autumn would most likely give the brightest red leaves?
questions.explanation: The passage says bright, sunny days and cool nights help trees make more red, so that weather gives the strongest reds.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention the thin layer of cells?
options: To show where chlorophyll is made
To describe how red color forms
To explain why leaves are green
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says the layer cuts each leaf off so it falls, letting the tree rest without losing water.
"country" fits. The paragraph is about why countries trade; "A country" is the subject.
"not" fits. "Need not be" means does not have to be; only "not" makes the negative.
"the" fits. "The best producer" needs the article before a superlative.
"producer" fits. A country is a producer of goods; "the best producer" is a noun phrase.
"good" fits. "A good" in economics is a product; the sentence later calls it "that product".
"it" fits. "Before it can profit" needs a subject pronoun for the country.
"profit" fits. After "can" a base verb is needed, and "profit from selling" means gain money by selling.
"selling" fits. "Profit from selling" needs a verb in -ing form after the preposition.
"product" fits. "That product" refers back to "a good".
"What" fits. "What matters is the cost" needs a pronoun that can be a subject.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what was a problem with animal bladders?
options: They changed the color of the paint
They made the paint dry more slowly
They leaked and were hard to carry
They were too expensive to buy
questions.explanation: The passage says bladders "leaked, burst and were awkward to carry".

questions.stem: The word "obstacle" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: The tube "removed a practical obstacle": it took away something that had stood in painters' way.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe how painters worked before 1841?
options: To criticize the use of animal products
To show what the tube made possible
To explain how pigments were invented
To argue that older paintings were better
questions.explanation: The first paragraph explains that landscapes were finished indoors; this sets up the point that the tube let painters work outdoors.

questions.stem: What does the passage suggest about the tube's role in Impressionism?
options: It was invented by an Impressionist
It was the main reason the style began
It had no effect on Impressionist painters
It helped the style but did not cause it
questions.explanation: The author says the tube "did not create a new style by itself, but it removed a practical obstacle", so it helped rather than caused the movement.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Impressionists is supported by the passage?
options: They wanted to record changing light
They preferred to paint portraits indoors
questions.explanation: They "wanted to record how light and weather changed from hour to hour"; the other options contradict the passage.
"ash" fits. "Ash from an eruption" is what settles on the ground and later "the ash" again.
"an" fits. "An eruption" needs the article before a noun that starts with a vowel sound.
"settles" fits. After the subject "ash" the clause needs a verb, and ash settles, or comes to rest.
"the" fits. "The ground" needs the article.
"it" fits. "It slowly breaks down" needs a subject pronoun for the ash.
"breaks" fits. Ash "breaks down" over time; a verb is needed after "slowly".
"and" fits. "Breaks down and releases" joins two verbs.
"the" fits. "The minerals" needs the article before the noun.
"that" fits. "Minerals that crops need" needs a relative pronoun to begin the clause.
"need" fits. Crops need minerals to grow; a verb is needed after "crops".
"believe" fits. "Scientists believe that" introduces what they think; a verb is needed.
"these" fits. "These birds" points back to the birds just mentioned.
"rely" fits. Birds "rely on" tools: they depend on them.
"several" fits. "Several different tools" means a few kinds; the passage goes on to list them.
"tools" fits. The passage lists ways of finding the way, which are the birds' tools.
"they" fits. "When they plan" needs a subject pronoun for the birds.
"their" fits. "Their routes" needs a possessive for the birds' own routes.
"Young" fits. "Young birds" contrasts with "older birds" later in the sentence.
"seem" fits. "Seem to know" needs a verb that takes "to".
"know" fits. Young birds "know the general direction" from birth.

questions.stem: When is the Hillside Branch open on Friday, November 27?
questions.explanation: The Hillside column shows "Closed" for Friday; noon to 6 p.m. is the Main Branch.

questions.stem: A book is due on Thursday, November 26. When is it due instead?
options: There is no new due date
questions.explanation: The note says items due while a branch is closed are due the next open day.

questions.stem: What does the schedule suggest a reader can do on Thanksgiving Thursday?
options: Return books in a book drop
Pick up books at the Main Branch
questions.explanation: Both branches are closed Thursday, but the book drops stay open every day, so returns are still possible.

questions.stem: Why did Greenleaf Outdoor write to Daniel?
options: To offer him a different tent
To explain a delay in his order
To confirm that his refund is complete
To ask him to pay extra shipping
questions.explanation: The email says the tent is out of stock while the other items have shipped, so its purpose is to explain a delay.
The rest of the order, "hiking socks and a water filter", shipped today and should arrive by Friday.

questions.stem: What should Daniel do if he does not want to wait for the tent?
questions.explanation: The email says to reply if he would rather not wait, and the tent will be refunded.
Hannah found the dog "near the playground on Elm and 3rd". Oak Street is the name of the neighbors' group.

questions.stem: Why does Hannah ask owners to tell her something not in the post?
options: To decide who should pay for a bath
To find out where the dog lives
To check they really own her
To learn the dog's name for a tag
questions.explanation: Anyone could repeat the details in the post, so asking for a new detail helps Hannah make sure the person really owns the dog.

questions.stem: According to the sign, which side of the lane should swimmers use?
questions.explanation: The sign says "Swim on the right side of the lane."

questions.stem: What does the sign imply about swimming at 10 p.m.?
options: Only the fast lane is open
questions.explanation: A lifeguard is on duty only until 9 p.m., and at other times people swim at their own risk, so the pool can be used but nobody is guarding it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how does a bat tell how far away an object is?
options: By which ear hears the call first
By the pitch of the insect's sound
By how loud its call is
By how long an echo takes
questions.explanation: The passage says the time an echo takes to return tells the distance; differences between the ears give direction instead.

questions.stem: The word "plentiful" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: Insects are "plentiful" at night: there are many of them.

questions.stem: Why does a bat call only a few times per second while searching?
options: It can scan a wide area
Its ears need time to rest
It saves its energy for flying
questions.explanation: The passage says the slow rate "lets it scan a wide area".

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the last paragraph?
options: To show prey can escape bats
To describe how bats learn to call
To explain why bats hunt at night
questions.explanation: It begins "Insects are not defenseless" and describes moths that dive or click to escape bats.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the clicking moths?
options: Bats may misjudge where they are
They cannot hear the calls of bats
questions.explanation: Their clicks "seem to interfere with the bat's ability to judge distance", so a bat may misjudge where they are.
"ago" fits. "Long ago" means a long time in the past.
"cost" fits. Books "cost a great deal": they were expensive.
"great" fits. "A great deal" means a lot of money.
"and" fits. "And only rich families" joins the two parts of the sentence.
"rich" fits. Only rich families could afford many expensive books.
"could" fits. "Could keep" needs a helping verb before the base verb "keep".
"large" fits. "Large collections" needs an adjective before the noun.
"at" fits. "At home" is the fixed phrase for in one's own house.
"As" fits. "As more workers learned" means while, or because, more of them learned.
"workers" fits. A plural noun for people is needed: workers learned to read.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what is demand?
options: The amount buyers want to buy
questions.explanation: The passage defines demand as "the amount that buyers want to buy"; the amount sellers are ready to sell is supply.

questions.stem: The word "scarce" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: A product that is scarce is one there is little of, which is why buyers compete for it.

questions.stem: Why are strawberries cheaper in early summer?
options: Shops pay farmers less in summer
Winter fruit is still in the shops
Nearby farms harvest a lot at once
questions.explanation: Farms near the city harvest large amounts at the same time, so supply is high and shops lower prices.

questions.stem: Why does the author discuss strawberries?
options: To compare summer and winter weather
To give an example of the two ideas
To argue that fruit is too expensive
To explain how berries are grown
questions.explanation: The author says "Strawberries are a good example" of how supply and demand change prices.

questions.stem: What would the author most likely expect after a year of high potato prices?
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says a high price signals that buyers pay well, so some farmers grow more of that crop the next year.
"and" fits. "Asphalt and concrete" joins the two subjects.
"absorb" fits. The two materials "absorb sunlight": they take it in, which is why they release heat later.
"during" fits. "During the day" tells when the sunlight is absorbed.
"day" fits. "The day" contrasts with "after dark".
"release" fits. The materials "absorb ... and release" heat: a base verb matching "absorb" is needed.
"stored" fits. "The stored heat" is heat kept from the day; it is released later.
"slowly" fits. An adverb is needed after "release the stored heat", and slow release keeps the air warm at night.
"dark" fits. "After dark" means after night falls.
"the" fits. "The air" needs the article.
"cools" fits. The air cools less overnight, which explains the warmer nights.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what had protected the soil in earlier dry periods?
options: Rows of trees planted by farmers
Plowing along the curves of the land
questions.explanation: The deep roots of native grasses "had anchored the light soil through earlier dry periods"; trees and curved plowing came later.

questions.stem: The word "anchored" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: Roots "anchored the light soil": they held it so the wind could not move it.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention rising wheat prices and new tractors?
options: To show that farming was easy in the 1930s
To argue that the drought was caused by people
To explain why so much grassland was plowed
To describe where the families moved
questions.explanation: They "encouraged farmers to plow millions of acres of native grassland", which left the soil exposed.

questions.stem: What does the passage suggest about the causes of the Dust Bowl?
options: The drought alone caused the dust storms
Drought did more harm on plowed land
Farmers had never faced dry years
questions.explanation: The author says the causes were "partly natural and partly human": the drought hit fields left bare by plowing, while grass-covered soil had survived earlier dry periods.

questions.stem: Which practice did the Soil Conservation Service promote?
options: Moving farms to the Atlantic coast
Plowing more land to grow wheat
questions.explanation: The service promoted tree rows, plowing along curves and "returning damaged fields to grass".
"their" fits. "Their leaves" means the plants' own leaves; a possessive is needed.
"green" fits. "Green cells" needs an adjective; the cells in leaves are green.
"capture" fits. After the subject "cells" a verb is needed: they capture, or catch, energy.
"from" fits. "Energy from light" says where the energy comes from.
"and" fits. "Capture ... and use" joins two verbs.
"it" fits. "Use it" needs an object pronoun for the energy.
"join" fits. "Join water with carbon dioxide" means combine them.
"with" fits. "Join water with carbon dioxide" needs a preposition.
"dioxide" fits. Carbon dioxide is the gas plants take from the air.
"in" fits. "Taken in from the air" means drawn into the leaf; "taken in" is the phrasal verb for absorbing something.
"rarely" fits. "Merchants rarely traveled" needs an adverb before the verb: they seldom went the whole way.
"its" fits. "Its full length" means the whole length of the Silk Road.
"length" fits. "Its full length" is the whole distance of the routes.
"most" fits. "Most goods" means the greater part of them.
"passed" fits. Goods "passed from one trader" to another: a past tense verb is needed.
"one" fits. "From one trader into the hands of another" pairs "one" with "another".
"into" fits. "Into the hands of another" needs a preposition of movement.
"hands" fits. "Into the hands of another" means into another trader's possession.
"another" fits. "Another" completes "from one trader ... another".
"the" fits. "Along the way" is a fixed phrase meaning during the journey.
"main" fits. "The main cables" are the biggest ones; the text repeats "the main cables" later.
"pass" fits. The cables "pass over tall towers": a verb is needed after the subject.
"tall" fits. "Tall towers" needs an adjective before the noun.
"and" fits. "Pass over ... and are fixed" joins two verbs.
"fixed" fits. "Are fixed firmly" needs a past participle: the cables are attached.
"in" fits. "Fixed firmly in the ground" needs a preposition before the noun phrase.
"ground" fits. The cables are anchored in the ground at each end.
"both" fits. "Both ends" means each of the two ends.
"of" fits. "Ends of the bridge" needs "of" to link the nouns.
"bridge" fits. The ends belong to the bridge being described.

questions.stem: What does the student membership NOT include?
options: Night use of the weight room
questions.explanation: Towel service is listed as extra. Classes, the climbing wall and 24-hour weight room access are included.

questions.stem: What is suggested about a student who joins in September?
options: They pay a fee after September 30
They can only visit during the day
They must join a class every week
questions.explanation: The ad says the price stays the same as long as you remain a student, so it will not go up while they study.

questions.stem: What must a student show to get the special price?
questions.explanation: The ad says to show a valid student ID.

questions.stem: Why did Professor Alvarez send the email?
options: To explain what replaces the class
To cancel the whole course for the week
To move the lab to a new room
questions.explanation: The professor will be at a conference, so the email explains what replaces Wednesday's class and when the quiz will be taken.

options: Wednesday at the end of class
questions.explanation: The quiz opens online Thursday and closes Friday at midnight.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the recorded lecture?
options: It will be shown in Lecture Hall B
It is only for students who miss the quiz
questions.explanation: Students are asked to watch it instead of attending Wednesday's class, so it stands in for that class.

questions.stem: What will Sam most likely buy for Lee?
questions.explanation: Lee asks for milk, and says to skip the rice because it is not on sale.

questions.stem: What does Lee mean by "Skip it then"?
questions.explanation: "Skip it" means leave it out; Lee does not want rice at full price.

questions.stem: How much did the student discount save?
questions.explanation: The discount is 10% of labor only: 10% of \$25.00 is \$2.50, as the invoice shows. 10% of the whole bill would have been more.

questions.stem: If the new screen stops working after two months, what is likely?
options: The customer pays the full price again
questions.explanation: Two months is within the 90-day warranty on parts, so the screen should be covered.
The notice says to use the temporary stop on Birch Street, one block north.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about March 15?
options: Buses stop at Pine Avenue again
Route 12 will stop running for good
questions.explanation: The detour lasts from March 3 to March 14, so the normal stop should return after that.
The page lists gloves, bags and snacks as provided; water bottles and shoes are for volunteers to bring.

questions.stem: Why should a large group email first?
options: To get a later start time
To be allowed to bring children
questions.explanation: Groups of more than five should email "so we can plan the tools".

questions.stem: According to the passage, what mainly causes tides?
questions.explanation: The passage says tides "are caused mainly by the gravity of the Moon"; the Sun's effect is less than half as strong.

options: When the Moon is farthest away
When the Sun and Moon are at right angles
When the Sun and Moon line up
questions.explanation: Spring tides happen at new and full moon, when the Sun and Moon line up; right angles give neap tides.

questions.stem: The word "bulges" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: The ocean "bulges slightly toward the Moon": it swells out in that direction.

questions.stem: Why does the author say spring tides "have nothing to do with the season"?
options: To explain why tides are strongest in spring
To introduce the topic of neap tides
To show that tides are hard to predict
questions.explanation: The name suggests the season, so the author clarifies that it refers to the Sun and Moon lining up, not to spring.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about a coast in a narrow bay?
options: It is not affected by the Moon
Its tides may rise very high
It has only one high tide a day
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says the shape of a coast can greatly increase the range, and in some narrow bays the water rises many meters.

questions.stem: The word "postpone" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: People "may postpone a choice that seems complicated": they put it off until later.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what differed between the two kinds of companies?
questions.explanation: The plan, benefits and effort were "almost identical"; only whether joining was the default differed.

questions.stem: Which is NOT given as a reason defaults are powerful?
questions.explanation: The passage gives attention, the default as a recommendation, and losses felt more sharply; cost is never mentioned.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe retirement savings plans?
options: To recommend a type of savings plan
To illustrate the effect of a default
To show that employees dislike forms
To explain how companies choose plans
questions.explanation: The author calls it "a well-known example" of how defaults shape behavior.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the author's conclusion?
questions.explanation: The last sentence says those who design forms "carry a responsibility to choose them with care".

questions.stem: According to the passage, why did New Orleans matter to early jazz?
options: It had the first recording studios
It was home to the first radio stations
questions.explanation: As a busy port, the city brought together people of different backgrounds "along with their musical traditions".

questions.stem: The word "improvised" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: The passage explains it at once: "creating new melodies on the spot".

questions.stem: In a typical early jazz band, which instrument carried the main tune?
questions.explanation: The cornet or trumpet carried the main tune while the clarinet and trombone wove lines around it.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the second paragraph?
options: Jazz changed how music was played
Jazz spread to Chicago and New York
questions.explanation: It says early players "also changed how the music was played" by improvising and playing several melodies at once.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about records and radio?
options: They helped jazz reach new audiences
questions.explanation: They carried the playing "to listeners who had never heard a live jazz band", spreading the music.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what are antibodies?
questions.explanation: The passage defines antibodies as "proteins that attach to the germ and help destroy it".

questions.stem: Why does a vaccinated person usually not become sick from the vaccine?
options: The dose is given over several days
questions.explanation: A vaccine uses a harmless version or a single part of a germ, which "cannot cause the disease".

questions.stem: The word "fades" in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: Booster doses are needed because memory "fades", becoming weaker over time.

questions.stem: How does the second paragraph relate to the first?
options: It disagrees with the first paragraph
It describes a different body system
It lists the symptoms of disease
It applies the idea of immune memory
questions.explanation: The first paragraph explains memory cells, and the second begins "Vaccines take advantage of this memory".

questions.stem: What can be inferred about newborn babies?
options: They need booster doses at birth
They depend on others being immune
questions.explanation: Babies who cannot be vaccinated are protected when enough people around them are immune, because the germ has trouble spreading.
